# The DPO loss

The paper's DPO objective is Eq. 7 **(p. 4)**:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\pi_{\theta};\pi_{\text{ref}})=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{w}\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{l}\mid x)}\right)\right]$$

The symbols mean the following:
- $y_w$ and $y_l$ are the preferred and dispreferred completions for prompt $x$ **(p. 3)**.
- $\sigma$ is the logistic function **(p. 3)**.
- $\beta$ controls how far the policy may drift from the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ **(p. 3)**.
- $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is normally the SFT model. If no SFT model is available, it is set by maximizing the likelihood of the preferred completions **(p. 4)**.
- By default $\beta = 0.1$. For TL;DR summarization they use $\beta = 0.5$ **(p. 19)**.

This loss has the same form as the reward-model loss in Eq. 2, $-\mathbb{E}[\log\sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l))]$ **(p. 3)**. The difference is that the policy log-ratio terms replace $r_\phi$ **(p. 4)**.

# What plays the role of the reward

The reward is an **implicit reward** defined by the policy and the reference model **(p. 4)**:

$$\hat{r}_{\theta}(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$$

There is no separately trained reward model. The paper says the policy network represents both the language model and the (implicit) reward **(p. 4)**.

**Why this works:**
1. The optimal policy for the KL-constrained objective is $\pi_r = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}\exp(r/\beta)$ (Eq. 4). Rearranging gives $r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_r}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}+\beta\log Z(x)$ (Eq. 5) **(p. 4)**.
2. The Bradley-Terry model depends only on the difference between two rewards. So when Eq. 5 is substituted, the $\beta\log Z(x)$ term cancels, leaving only the policy terms **(p. 4)**.
3. This reparameterization loses no generality. Every reward equivalence class consistent with Bradley-Terry or Plackett-Luce can be written as $\beta\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ (Theorem 1, **p. 6**; full proof on **p. 18**). Rewards that differ only by a function of $x$ give the same preferences and the same optimal policy (Lemmas 1–2, **p. 5**).

The gradient shows how this reward is used during training. Each example is weighted by $\sigma(\hat{r}_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat{r}_\theta(x,y_w))$, so examples where the implicit reward ranks the pair wrongly get more weight. The update then raises the likelihood of $y_w$ and lowers that of $y_l$ **(p. 4)**. The authors report that removing this weighting can cause the model to degenerate **(p. 4)**.

**A note on Appendix A.4 (p. 17):** Eq. 21 writes the sigmoid argument with $y_l$ and $y_w$ swapped compared with Eq. 7. The final gradient on the same page matches the main-text form, so the swap appears to be a typo.
